cues.en: My name's Bob Felderman, and I work in the platform networking group here. And I have the pleasure today to introduce this morning's speaker, Van Jacobson. For a lot of you, I presume Van needs no introduction, but I can't resist going ahead and saying a few things. Van's been working for a lot of years on some of the most interesting and most difficult problems in networking.
cues.zh: 我叫 Bob Felderman，在平台网络组工作。今天很高兴介绍今早的演讲者 Van Jacobson。对很多人来说，我猜 Van 无需介绍，但我忍不住还是想说几句。Van 多年来一直研究网络领域一些最有趣也最困难的问题。

cues.en: And really beginning with his seminal paper, which a lot of you probably read, called Congestion, Avoidance, and Control, which was a SIGCOM paper in 1988. He's authored dozens of papers in RFCs and been working in this area for a long time.
cues.zh: 真正要从他 1988 年那篇 SIGCOM 论文说起，叫 Congestion, Avoidance, and Control，你们很多人可能读过。他在 RFC 中撰写了几十篇论文，在这个领域工作了很久。

cues.en: In addition to having big ideas and solving a lot of theoretical problems, Van is one of those rare people who can also really get down into the code and really solve the problem at the bits and bytes level. He's contributed to a lot of tools that you probably use every day if you're in the networking area, things like traceroute, pathchart, TCP dump, and many other things.
cues.zh: 除了有宏大想法、解决许多理论问题之外，Van 还是那种少有的人，能真正深入代码，在比特和字节层面真正解决问题。他为很多工具做出了贡献，如果你在网络领域，可能每天都在用，比如 traceroute、pathchart、TCP dump 等等。

cues.en: Many of you are no doubt familiar with the VGA header compression, which was originally used on low speed links, but still exists in lots of networking technology today. And back when Van was at LBL, Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory, he was one of the leaders in creating what was called the M-Bone or the multicast backbone and developing a lot of tools.
cues.zh: 你们很多人肯定都熟悉 VGA 报头压缩，它最初用于低速链路，但如今仍存在于大量网络技术中。当年 Van 在 LBL，也就是劳伦斯伯克利实验室时，他是创建所谓 M-Bone（多播主干网）并开发大量工具的领军人物之一。

cues.en: Things like, some of you may remember, Vic and Vat and WB. They were audio, video, and shared whiteboard over the internet long before people believed this kind of stuff was even possible. In the past few years, Van's work has been recognized with things like the 2001 SIGCOMM Award, the 2002 IEEE Kobayashi Award, and in 2004, he was elected to the National Academy of Engineering. And generally, they were citing
cues.zh: 比如有些人可能还记得的 Vic、Vat 和 WB。它们是互联网上的音频、视频和共享白板，远在人们相信这类东西可行之前就已出现。过去几年，Van 的工作获得了 2001 年 SIGCOMM Award、2002 年 IEEE Kobayashi Award 等认可，并在 2004 年当选美国国家工程院院士。而总的来说，他们表彰的是

cues.en: major contributions to the understanding of network congestion, the development of congestion control mechanisms, enabling the successful scaling of the internet. And he's really, really widely been credited with preventing the congestion collapse of the internet in the late 80s and early 90s. So I think Google probably owes Van a vote of thanks, because we might not even exist today if the internet hadn't been able to survive that scaling. And on a quick personal note, I just wanted to
cues.zh: 对理解网络拥塞、开发拥塞控制机制以及让互联网成功扩展所作出的重大贡献。而且人们普遍认为，是他防止了 80 年代末 90 年代初互联网的拥塞崩溃。所以我觉得 Google 可能得好好感谢 Van，因为如果互联网没能挺过那次扩展，我们甚至可能根本不会存在。另外，简单说点个人感受，我只是想

cues.en: point out that I had the good fortune to work closely with VAN over the last four or so years prior to I joined Google. And frankly, I've never seen anyone who could learn so much about what's going on in a network topology or between two hosts simply using a TCP dump file.
cues.zh: 指出，在我加入 Google 之前的四年左右时间里，我有幸与 Van 密切合作。坦率地说，我从未见过任何人能仅凭一个 tcpdump 文件，就对网络拓扑中或两台主机之间正在发生的情况了解得这么多。

cues.en: an aux script, and the simplest little graphing program I've ever seen. And it's just amazed me. I used to take our software team over. It was kind of the pilgrimage over to Van's office to kind of have him read the tea leaves for us. And we could look at the graph, and he would say, see, it's obvious. This is a Linux box talking to a Solaris box, and it's dropping packets here, and it's doing this and retransmitting. And wow, if we could only figure out how to do that, it'd be great.
cues.zh: 一个 aux 脚本，还有我见过的最简单的小型绘图程序。这真让我惊叹。我以前常带我们软件团队过去，那简直像是去 Van 的办公室朝圣，让他替我们解读天机。我们可以看着图，他会说，看，很明显。这是一台 Linux 机器在和一台 Solaris 机器通信，它在这里丢包，然后又这样那样、重传。哇，要是我们也能搞明白怎么做就好了，那就太棒了。

cues.en: One note, this is being recorded. It will go up on Google Video. So if you have questions at the end, if they are the least bit confidential or are talking about internal Google kinds of things, let's hold those questions until the videotaping is done and we can talk afterwards over lunch. And now, without any further ado, Van Jacobson.
cues.zh: 提醒一下，这段正在录像，之后会发布到 Google Video 上。所以如果最后你们有问题，只要稍微涉及机密，或者是在谈 Google 内部的事情，就先留到录像结束，之后我们午餐时再聊。现在，闲话少说，有请 Van Jacobson。

cues.en: A really pompous title for what's going to be a really pompous talk. It's a hard talk to give. The motivation behind it is, it seems to me for at least the last decade, network research in the US has been really stuck in a dead end. It should be just a wonderful time for networking because we've got everything connected to everything else. We've got ubiquitous, wireless.
cues.zh: 这个标题很浮夸，接下来的演讲也会很浮夸。这是一场很难讲的演讲。背后的动机是，在我看来，至少过去十年，美国的网络研究真的陷入了死胡同。本来这该是网络研究的黄金时期，因为所有东西都互联了。我们有无处不在的无线。

cues.en: phones that are starting to show up on the internet. We've got this huge wealth of information that was created by the web. We have things like Google that are indexing to make it easy to find stuff. But every day, everything we're doing with the network gets harder. Wireless just barely works. If you're on a campus, you can make it work. If you're wandering around, it doesn't. Every one of us has spread over multiple devices.
cues.zh: 手机开始出现在互联网上。Web 创造了海量信息。我们有 Google 这样的东西在做索引，让查找资料变得容易。但每一天，我们用网络做的每件事都变得更难。无线只是勉强能用。在校园里还能用；四处走动就不行。我们每个人都分散在多个设备上。

cues.en: two laptops, two desktops, home computer, phone. None of them are ever in sync. None of them have the information that I need on them when I need it. And the tools that are coming out to help solve those problems are really ad hoc. They're kind of point tools. And it seems like there's got to be an architectural problem, because a problem seemed to be so ubiquitous. I think there was a similar time.
cues.zh:
两台笔记本、两台台式机、家用电脑、手机。
它们从来不同步。
我需要信息的时候，它们上面都没有我需要的那些信息。
而市面上帮助解决这些问题的工具，其实都很临时拼凑。
它们算是单点工具。
看来一定存在架构问题，因为这个问题似乎无处不在。
我觉得曾有过类似的时期。

cues.en: in the 60s and 70s, where there was a view of what networking was. That was basically networking was telephony, because communications in the 60s and 70s for almost all of the 20th century communications was telephony. And people were trying to make data work over telephony. And they just failed miserably, because data is not telephony, and telephony is not the only way of communications.
cues.zh:
在六七十年代，当时对网络是什么有一种看法。
基本上，网络就是电话通信，因为六七十年代——几乎整个20世纪的通信——都是电话通信。
人们当时想让数据跑在电话通信上。
结果他们惨败，因为数据不是电话通信，电话通信也不是唯一的通信方式。

cues.en: And I think we're stuck in a similar thing. It's not that the solution we've got, that the internet is a bad solution. It's just the problem has changed. And so we're in a world, it's kind of like the Copernican Revolution. We put the Earth at the center of the universe, and we're trying to figure out planetary motion. And you can do it, but it's just incredibly complicated, because your point of view is wrong. The Earth isn't at the center of the universe.
cues.zh: 我觉得我们也卡在类似的情况里。并不是我们现有的方案——互联网——是个糟糕的方案。只是问题已经变了。所以我们所处的世界，有点像哥白尼革命。我们把地球放在宇宙中心，试图弄明白行星运动。你能做到，但会极其复杂，因为你的视角错了。地球并不在宇宙中心。

cues.en: And if you make a little bit of change and put at least the sun at the center of the solar system, then suddenly everything gets a lot simpler. Both systems explain stuff, but one is just a lot simpler and a lot easier to work in. And I think we're kind of on the fringes of a Copernican revolution in communication. And I'm going to try to motivate that.
cues.zh: 而如果你稍作改变，至少把太阳放到太阳系中心，突然一切就简单多了。两套体系都能解释现象，但其中一套就是简单得多，也更容易在其中工作。我觉得我们差不多处在通信领域一场哥白尼革命的边缘。接下来我会试着说明为什么。

cues.en: I'm an old fart. They say when you get too old to think, you reminisce. So I'm going to try and motivate it by reminiscing about some history about that 60s and 70s change, trying to relate it to what I think is happening now. So starting turn of the century with the phone system, I had spent 20 years talking to telco people in the process of
cues.zh: 我是个老家伙。人们说，人老到没法思考时，就会怀旧。所以我想通过回顾60年代和70年代那场变革的一些历史来引出主题，并试着把它和我认为现在正在发生的事联系起来。那就从世纪之交的电话系统说起吧——我曾花了20年，在这个过程中和电信公司的人交谈，

cues.en: trying to work out the internet protocol. And it's a completely different mindset. And it took a long time for me to figure out that the phone system isn't about making calls. That's what we use it for. But that has nothing to do with the system. The system is about wires. And if you think of its context when it was created back in 1870, there were no wires.
cues.zh: 试图弄明白互联网协议。那是一种完全不同的思维方式。我花了很长时间才明白，电话系统并不是为了打电话。打电话只是我们使用它的方式。但那和这个系统本身毫无关系。这个系统的核心是线路。想想它1870年被创造时的背景——那时根本没有线路。

cues.en: The goal of the system, what Bell had to do to make a telephone system, was get wires everywhere. And it's enormously costly to do that. You need land. You need right away. You've got to pull the pair. And you're not making any money while you're doing that. It's all sunk costs. So what he had to design was a business model in the system that would get ubiquitous wires. And as soon as he got that, as soon as there were a lot of wires to connect to phones, then he could start making revenue by people making calls.
cues.zh: 这个系统的目标，也就是 Bell 要做电话系统必须完成的事，就是让线路铺得到处都是。而这件事成本极高。你需要土地。你需要路权。你得敷设线对。而且做这些的时候你还赚不到钱。全是沉没成本。所以他必须设计出一种商业模式，让系统能拥有无处不在的线路。一旦做到这一点，一旦有大量线路可以接到电话上，他就能靠人们打电话开始赚钱。

cues.en: With that focus, the thing that people are doing with your system and what the system does inside are completely different. The calls that you make are 100% side effect. And what the system is doing is trying to build a path through its wire matrix. And this causes a little bit of cognitive dissonance when you're talking to telco people, at least it did for me.
cues.zh: 在这种关注点下，人们用你的系统做的事，和系统内部实际做的事，完全是两回事。你打的电话 100% 是副作用。而系统真正在做的，是试图在它的线路矩阵中建立一条路径。这会在你跟电信行业的人交流时带来一点认知失调，至少对我来说是这样。

cues.en: I think of the endpoints. I pick up my phone, and I'm calling my mom in Phoenix. And I think of her phone number as the name of her phone. And I want to talk to the phone named Mom's phone. For telco, it's not that at all. The phone number is a program that you're sticking into the system to build a path through the wires. And that's how they view it internally. See if I can make that more concrete. So when I was growing up, this was how phones work.
cues.zh: 我会想到端点。我拿起手机，给在凤凰城的妈妈打电话。我把她的电话号码当成她手机的名字。我想和那台叫“妈妈的手机”的手机通话。但对电信运营商来说，完全不是这么回事。电话号码是你塞进系统里的一个程序，用来在电线中建立一条路径。他们内部就是这么看的。看看我能不能讲得更具体些。我小时候，电话就是这么工作的。

cues.en: You pick up the line. You say, I'd like to talk to 1234. And some operator goes, 1234. So that's column 12 row 34. They walk over on their switchboard and they plug in a jack. And they're connecting your wire to a particular outgoing line. So the phone number's at 2D coordinate on this switch matrix. There were some human factors work that said one person can reach 100,000 wires. They can conveniently work in a 10 by 100 grid. And so that's why we got four digit numbers.
cues.zh: 你拿起电话说，我想接通 1234。接线员就说，1234，也就是第 12 列第 34 行。他们走到交换机前，插上塞头，把你的线路接到某条特定的外线上。所以电话号码就是交换矩阵上的一个二维坐标。有人因工程研究表明，一个人能处理 10 万根线，在 10×100 的网格里操作比较方便。所以就有了四位数号码。

cues.en: So this is another way of finding a path through the system. This is from the first telephone switch, stronger switch. MIT used these up until 1990, I think. They were invented in 1890. So you've got one wire coming in at the bottom. You've got a 10 by 10 switch matrix. Every time you dial a pulse.
cues.zh: 这是最早的电话交换机，Strowger 交换机。MIT 一直用到 1990 年，我记得。它们是 1890 年发明的。底部有一根线进来。有一个 10×10 交换矩阵。每当你拨出一个脉冲。

cues.en: The switch clicks over one. So you dial a one. It'll click over one. If there's a long pause, it locks. And then when it gets the next pulse, it'll drop down one for each. So you're picking a 2D coordinate, two digits in, picking one of 100 output wires. And you cascade two of these. You can do the four-digit 10,000 lines. You had an end office. But your number, again, it's a program for this switch.
cues.zh: 交换机咔哒一声步进一格。你拨 1，它就步进一格。如果停顿太久，它就锁定。之后每收到一个脉冲，它就下降一格。所以你是在选一个二维坐标，输入两位数字，从 100 根输出线里选一根。把两个这样的交换机级联起来，就能处理四位数、10,000 条线路。你就有了一个端局。但你的号码，再说一次，就是这台交换机的程序。

cues.en: It has nothing whatsoever to do with the phone that you're calling. It has to do with connecting wires going through the system. So this works. Completely revolutionized communication. It did it as a side effect, but it was the only way it could have been done given the economic constraints. You had to get the wires in place. You had to make this base communication system.
cues.zh: 这跟你正在拨打的电话毫无关系。它关乎贯穿整个系统的连接线路。所以这奏效了。彻底革新了通信。它是作为副作用做到的，但在当时的经济约束下，这是唯一可行的做法。你必须把线路铺设到位。你必须建立这套基础通信系统。

cues.en: And then you had to figure out how to efficiently use those wires. Perfect. It's got some structural problems if you try to take it out of the context of people making calls to other people. One issue that Judge Green solved for us in the 70s was, if your world is building paths, you have to know all of the resources and you have to have control of all the resources. Because what you're doing.
cues.zh: 然后你必须想办法高效利用这些线路。完美。如果你把它从人们互相打电话的语境中抽离出来，它就有一些结构性问题。Judge Green 在 70 年代为我们解决的一个问题是：如果你的世界是在构建路径，你就必须知道所有资源，并且必须控制所有资源。因为这就是你在做的事。

cues.en: to make a call is finding unused pass segments and chaining them together. And if somebody else owns those pass segments and doesn't let you grab them and chain them together, or if they're assigned into a different call, you're host. And remember that we started this in the days of relays and people plugging jacks into patchboards.
cues.zh: 打一通电话，就是找到未使用的通路段，再把它们串接起来。如果这些通路段归别人所有，不让你占用并串接，或者它们已经被分配到另一通电话里，那你就彻底没戏了。还要记住，我们最早是在继电器时代、人们把插头插进配线板的年代开始做这件事的。

cues.en: There wasn't any electronics. There weren't any databases. There weren't any computers. You have to have something that starts working in this very primitive technology, and then you scale it through about a century. And by the time you get to the 60s, you've got electronics. You could start to decentralize things, but you've got all of this infrastructure and a big, powerful company set up. And it really wants to be a centralized monopoly, because it knows how to work efficiently in that way. And that was true all over the world.
cues.zh: 当时没有任何电子设备。没有数据库。没有计算机。你得先有某种能在这种非常原始的技术下运转起来的东西，然后用大约一个世纪去扩展它。到了60年代，你有了电子设备。你本可以开始去中心化，但你已经有了所有这些基础设施，还有一家庞大而强大的公司架构。它真的很想成为集中式垄断，因为它知道那样运作效率高。当时全世界都是如此。

cues.en: Even phone companies that started out fairly decentralized turned into big centralized monopolies. A big issue for the military in the 60s and 70s was we're worried about somebody dropping a bomb in the US. Is our phone system going to go down? The answer is yeah, almost certainly. Lots of things will go down. But this system in particular is really structurally unreliable.
cues.zh: 就连最初相当去中心化的电话公司，也变成了大型集中式垄断企业。60、70 年代军方的一大担忧是：要是有人往美国扔一颗炸弹怎么办？我们的电话系统会不会瘫痪？答案是：会，几乎肯定会。很多东西都会瘫痪。但这个系统尤其从结构上就非常不可靠。

cues.en: Because you're concatenating together a whole bunch of things, and they all have to work all the time in order for the system to work. That means that the reliability, which is the product of the failure probability of all of those elements that's going up exponentially, put in things in series, the probability of failure is p to the n. That's a problem. Back when I was doing control systems in the 70s, Bell Labs
cues.zh: 因为你是把一大堆东西串在一起，而它们必须一直全都正常工作，整个系统才能工作。这意味着可靠性——也就是所有那些元素故障概率的乘积——会指数级变化；把东西串联起来，故障概率就是 p 的 n 次方。这是个问题。70 年代我做控制系统的时候，贝尔实验室

cues.en: was the world's repository of information on reliability and how to build reliable systems. They couldn't actually do reliable systems. What they would do is reliable elements. Their switches were all gold plated. They would work forever. They all had modular redundant components and voters inside them. So if one thing failed, the other two would take over and work. They had to do this because their system was just incredibly unreliable.
cues.zh: 曾是全世界关于可靠性以及如何构建可靠系统的信息宝库。但他们其实做不出可靠的系统。他们做的是可靠的元件。他们的交换机全都镀了金，能用一辈子。里面都有模块化冗余组件和表决器。所以如果一个东西坏了，另外两个会接替工作。他们不得不这样做，因为他们的系统实在太不可靠了。

cues.en: And the only way that they could scale it up to a national size was to make individual elements that were incredibly reliable. It's kind of the opposite of the internet philosophy or the raid philosophy, the philosophy you use in your service, which take a bunch of cheap components, replicate them, allow some loose agreement between them. And if one fails, you don't give a damn, because there's lots of others. So you've got a system that's structurally reliable. You don't worry much about component reliability.
cues.zh: 他们能把它扩展到全国规模的唯一办法，就是让每个独立元件都极其可靠。这跟互联网理念或 RAID 理念正好相反——也就是你在服务里用的那套理念：拿一堆廉价组件，复制它们，让它们之间保持某种松散的共识。坏了一个也无所谓，因为还有很多别的。这样你得到的是一个结构上可靠的系统，不太用担心组件可靠性。

cues.en: So they're on the other end of the scale. And then the thing that really killed us when we started to do data, which is phone calls are this two-phase thing, because the system is all about building paths. So there's the part where you dial and connect to the far side, and you're building a path through the system. And while you're building that path, the things that kind of building a bridge across a river, and you're standing on it to build the next section.
cues.zh: 所以他们处在另一个极端。而当我们开始做数据业务时，真正把我们害惨的是：电话呼叫是两阶段的过程，因为整个系统就是围绕建立路径来设计的。也就是先拨号并连接到对端，你正在系统中建立一条路径。而建这条路径的过程，就像在河上建桥，你得站在已建好的部分上去建下一段。

cues.en: Everything behind you is all committed, but nobody can use it because you haven't made the bridge yet. So that's not an issue for phone calls, where you can build the path in about a second and the call lasts for at least a minute. So that's a 1% cost to build a path. But if you're sending data packets, a second's a long time. So typical transcontinental setup times is, best case, about 100 milliseconds.
cues.zh: 你身后的所有东西都已经提交好了，但没人能用，因为你还没搭好桥。对电话来说这不是问题，建立路径大约一秒，通话至少持续一分钟，所以建路径只有 1% 的成本。但发数据包时，一秒太长了。典型跨洲建立时间最好情况下约为 100 毫秒。

cues.en: So 100 milliseconds at a gigabit per second is 12 megabytes. That means that if you used a phone network, you would have to fetch 12 megabyte web pages to use the system at 50% efficiency. No web page is 12 megabytes big. You can't do what we do with networks when you have these huge setup costs to amortize. Because as the speed goes up, the amount of
cues.zh: 所以，在每秒 1 吉比特的速率下，100 毫秒就是 12 MB。这意味着，如果你用电话网络，就得获取 12 MB 的网页，才能以 50% 的效率使用这个系统。没有网页有 12 MB 那么大。当你要摊销这些巨大的建立成本时，你没法像我们在网络里那样做。因为随着速度提高，……的量

cues.en: bandwidth of potential data that you're throwing away waiting for your connection to get set up is enormous. It's getting on the order of gigabytes. And we don't want to talk in units that are that big. Typically, we want to get some information. That tells us what to get next. So there was a bunch of work that was happening in the 60s and 70s saying, oh, here's the core problem.
cues.zh: 等待连接建立期间被丢弃的潜在数据带宽非常巨大，已经达到 GB 量级。我们不想用那么大的单位来讨论。通常，我们想获取一些信息，用来告诉我们接下来该获取什么。所以在 60、70 年代有大量工作出现，说：这就是核心问题。

cues.en: We're either going to get a data network like ISDN. 64 kilobits is all God ever intended you to have. And if you make it slow enough, then the holding time really doesn't matter. And a bit's 10 miles long at 64 kilobits, so it only takes a few to go across country.
cues.zh: 我们要么会得到像 ISDN 这样的数据网络。64 kbps 就是上帝打算让你拥有的全部带宽。只要把它做得足够慢，占用时间就真的无所谓了。而且在 64 kbps 下，一个比特有 10 英里长，所以横跨全国只需要几个比特。

cues.en: But if we ever wanted to make a faster network, we had to figure out how to do faster setups. And so pretty much the entire US research establishment was aimed at that problem. Networking research was how to amortize the setup costs, and maybe we should worry about the reliability and some of the other structural things. But it went as an unspoken, unquestionable assumption that telephony was the right model for data networking.
cues.zh: 但如果我们想做出更快的网络，就必须搞清楚如何更快地建立连接。于是，几乎整个美国研究界都瞄准了这个问题。网络研究的重点是如何摊薄建立成本，也许还应该担心可靠性和其他一些结构性问题。但有一个心照不宣、不容置疑的假设：电话是数据网络的正确模型。

cues.en: It was communication. Nobody did anything else. But there are these two guys, Paul Barron, Don Davies, Barron at Rand Corporation in LA, but he now lives in the Bay Area. Don Davies in the UK. They said, what if telephony is not the only way to communicate? There were other things. There were signal flags.
cues.zh: 这就是通信。没人做别的事。但有两个人，Paul Barron 和 Don Davies——Barron 在洛杉矶的 Rand Corporation，不过他现住在湾区；Don Davies 在英国。他们说，如果电话不是唯一的通信方式呢？还有别的方式。还有信号旗。

cues.en: Morse code. Through history, we've seen people doing lots of different styles of communication. Maybe we can adapt something other than the telephony conversational paradigm. And so they were free to change their point of view because Bell had put in a whole bunch of wires. And so they didn't have to worry about the problem of, well, how am I going to get a communication path between two computers?
cues.zh: 摩尔斯电码。纵观历史，人们采用过许多不同的通信方式。也许我们可以采用电话式会话范式之外的其他方式。也正因此，他们可以自由地改变视角，因为贝尔已经铺设了大量线路。于是他们不必担心这个问题：我该如何在两台计算机之间建立一条通信路径？

cues.en: Just take it as given. There is a communication path. There's lots. The phone system's in place. Just use it. It's there. Let's split data up into little pieces, because there's not an infinite number of wires between any two places. Not everything is connected with its own individual pairs of wires. So we're going to have to share the path. The only way that we could share the path among many things is to have the amount of work that we do per thing be controlled.
cues.zh: 就把它当作既定条件。通信路径是存在的。而且有很多。电话系统已经就绪。直接用就行。它就在那儿。让我们把数据拆成小块，因为任意两个地点之间的线路数量并不是无限的。并不是每样东西都有自己单独的一对线路相连。所以我们必须共享路径。要在多个事物之间共享路径，唯一的办法就是控制我们为每个事物所做的工作量。

cues.en: If somebody can send a gigabyte into the path and I can't do anything until that gigabyte has gone away, it's like mixing cars and trains on the city roadway system, you're going to spend a lot of time in your car waiting at an intersection for a train to go by. You don't want to do that. You want to have limited length things. It would be nice here to not have big trucks. It would be just little cars.
cues.zh: 如果有人能往路径里塞进 1GB 数据，而在这 1GB 走完之前我什么都做不了，那就像把汽车和火车混在城市道路上：你会花很多时间坐在车里，在路口等火车过去。你不想这样。你希望传输的东西长度有限。这里最好不要有大卡车，只有小汽车就好了。

cues.en: So Davey said, hey yeah, chop it up into little pieces. We'll call them packets. And then Paul had this cool idea. His background was a mathematician. He said, let's use transitivity to get things together. So if you get one of these chunks of data, and it's got in its header where it's going, and if it's not you, then figure out how to send it on.
cues.zh: 所以 Davey 说，好啊，把它切成小块。我们叫它们数据包。然后 Paul 有个很酷的想法。他是数学家出身。他说，我们用传递性把东西串起来。于是，如果你收到一块数据，它的头部写着要去哪里，而目的地不是你，那就想办法把它继续转发出去。

cues.en: And I don't know how to figure out how to send it on, but I know I could statically configure that to get us started, and then we could figure out how to do it more dynamically. So this is a wonderful property, right? This graph theory, if you do a closure on a graph, almost any graph is completely connected as soon as it gets more than one edge per node on the average.
cues.zh: 我还不知道该怎么把它继续转发出去，但我知道可以先静态配置一下，让我们起步，然后再研究怎么做得更动态。所以这是个很棒的性质，对吧？在图论里，如果你对一个图做闭包，几乎任何图只要平均每个节点超过一条边，就会变成完全连通。

cues.en: through your brand of graphs says, hey, you've got the whole thing connected. And so if you've got transitivity built into this system, you don't need to engineer it. You just need to hook it up, and it's going to work. So they wrote about this. Paul in particular published this in 64 in IEEE transactions on communications. Utter heresy. Everybody who did communications, the entire staff of Bell Labs,
cues.zh: 通过你这类图，它会说：嘿，整个东西已经连通了。所以如果这个系统内置了传递性，你就不需要再去工程化实现它。你只要把它接起来，它就能工作。所以他们写了这件事。特别是 Paul 在 64 年把这篇发在 IEEE Transactions on Communications 上。简直是异端。所有搞通信的人，整个贝尔实验室的员工，

cues.en: came out and said, this can't possibly work. He's ignored everything that makes the phone system work, that makes it scale, that makes it reliable. Fortunately, there was this guy, James Licklitter, director of ARPA at the time, who knew nothing about networking, but he kind of liked the paper.
cues.zh: 都出来说，这根本不可能行得通。他忽略了让电话系统能运作、能扩展、能可靠的一切。幸运的是，有个人，James Licklitter，当时的 ARPA 主任，他对网络一无所知，但他还挺喜欢那篇论文。

cues.en: BBN to build the network that Paul Barron had written about. And they turned it on in September 71, and it worked like a champ. Now, it was built on top of the existing phone system. It never could have been built if it didn't have those wires available. It was using those wires. It was using them in a different way than the phone company was using them.
cues.zh: BBN 负责建造 Paul Barron 曾写到的那个网络。他们在 71 年 9 月把它启动，运行得非常好。它建立在现有电话系统之上。如果没有那些现成线路，它根本不可能被建出来。它用的就是那些线路，只是用法和电话公司不同。

cues.en: It assumed that the phone company is going to build this little path. That's what it does really well. And we ignore that. And wherever the bits happen to get, that's where they get. And then the node will figure out where they need to get to next. And so it was a network that hooked itself together as a mesh and figured out you only had to worry about connecting adjacent hops. And it's going to figure out the rest. So you couldn't make the network without Bell's work. You needed to be able to put bits into it. They didn't really care.
cues.zh: 它假定电话公司会铺好这一小段路径。那是电话公司很擅长的事，而我们不去管它。比特到了哪里，就算哪里。然后节点会判断它们接下来该去哪里。所以这是一个能把自己连成网状、并发现你只需关心相邻跳的网络。其余的它会自己搞定。所以没有 Bell 的工作，就做不出这个网络。你需要能把比特放进去。他们并不真的在意。

cues.en: How fast or how slow you put the bits in. Nice thing about the design was it's completely speed agnostic, unlike the phone system network. So they took whatever crummy modems they could get at the time, which were 56 kilobit acoustic couplers. It was passing packets pretty much from day one. The ideas were so simple they couldn't fail. But if you look at it, all the telco people said with very loud voices, that's not a network.
cues.zh: 你以多快或多慢的速度把比特送进去。这个设计的妙处在于它完全与速度无关，不像电话系统网络。所以他们当时能弄到什么破调制解调器就用什么，也就是 56 千比特的声耦合器。它几乎从第一天起就在传数据包。这些想法简单到不可能失败。但你要是细看，所有电信运营商的人都大声说：那根本不算网络。

cues.en: That's just a crummy way to use our network. You're taking our wires, you're sending on the paths that we create, and you're putting a lot of extra gunk on it so that you use it really inefficiently. And that's always going to be the case. When Copernicus first wrote his paper on planetary motions, the predictions that he gave were really crummy compared to the Ptolemaic predictions. The Earth-centered universe
cues.zh: 那只是使用我们网络的一种糟糕方式。你们占用我们的线路，沿着我们创建的路径发送，还在上面加一大堆多余的东西，结果用得极其低效。而且情况永远会是这样。Copernicus 最初写行星运动论文时，他给出的预测跟 Ptolemaic 的预测相比真的很糟糕。地心宇宙的

cues.en: astronomers had had three centuries to work out the math of that, and they'd gotten really, really good at it. And this new system comes along. It's one week old, and hey, it sort of tells you where stuff is, but don't set your compass by it. It's pretty crummy stuff. And so you've got this new packet network. It's a pure overlay.
cues.zh: 天文学家们有三个世纪的时间把那套数学研究透，已经非常非常擅长了。然后这个新系统出现了。它才诞生一周，嘿，它大概能告诉你东西在哪儿，但别拿它来校准指南针。这东西相当糟糕。于是你有了这个新的分组网络。它是个纯粹的覆盖网络。

cues.en: It is really inefficient compared to the telephony network. The telephony network didn't have anything like addresses in it. They were all implicit. And it took a long time. It took like 10 years to most people could look at that network and see the IP network. Really, it didn't matter.
cues.zh: 跟电话网络相比，它确实非常低效。电话网络里根本没有地址这种东西，一切都是隐含的。而且这花了很长时间。大概过了10年，大多数人才终于能看着那个网络，看出IP网络。其实，这并不重要。

cues.en: whether it was over a phone network or over an ethernet or over a token ring or over a satellite or over a radio, it was really completely agnostic about the delivery technology. And you really shouldn't care that it was an overlay. One of its features was it could be overlaid on damn near anything. And if you got hung up and, oh, but this is just an overlay and the real network is underneath it, you missed the whole point. The point was they changed the point of view. They were looking at the endpoints and not at the paths. And when you do that, you can make this agnostic network.
cues.zh: 无论是跑在电话网络、以太网、令牌环、卫星还是无线电上，它都完全不关心底层传输技术。而且你真的不该在意它是个覆盖网络。它的一个特点就是几乎可以叠加在任何东西上。如果你纠结于“哦，但这只是个覆盖层，真正的网络在它下面”，那你就完全错过了重点。重点是，他们改变了视角。他们看的是端点，而不是路径。这样做，你就能做出这种不依赖底层技术的网络。

cues.en: But at the time, they didn't convince anybody. The entire research community was still driving the truck down this road of, how can we do fast setup? How can we do fast connections? Almost the entire research community. So there were these two other guys, Stanford professors. All the networking had been done on the East Coast. These two guys.
cues.zh: 但当时他们没能说服任何人。整个研究界还在沿着这条路猛开卡车：怎么快速建立连接？怎么快速连通？几乎整个研究界都是如此。所以还有另外两个人，是斯坦福的教授。此前所有网络研究都在东海岸做。就是这两个人。

cues.en: The ARPANET was this massive success. It just worked. Everybody wanted one. Everybody wanted to communicate with that kind of technology. And so a dozen different military organizations, a dozen different academic groups, they were all building their own networks. They all had to sort of piss on it and make it there. So all the protocols are different. All the encapsulations are different. All the addressing structure is different. But the idea is they're all packet switch networks. And Vint looked at it and said,
cues.zh: ARPANET 取得了巨大成功。它就是能跑。每个人都想要一个。每个人都想用这种技术通信。于是十几个不同的军事组织、十几个不同的学术团体，都在建自己的网络。他们都得各自插一脚、搞出自己的版本。所以协议各不相同。封装各不相同。寻址结构也各不相同。但本质上，它们都是分组交换网络。Vint 看了看说：

cues.en: Oh, we could catenate these networks. If you've got a phone network where you're building paths, the topological details are all that matters. So you have to have detailed knowledge of the topology and detailed knowledge of how the links are assigned. When you're building a packet network, when you apply Paul's ideas, the topology doesn't matter. Nothing could be more irrelevant. The topology is something that a packet sees at the instant that it's going through a network.
cues.zh: 哦，我们可以把这些网络串联起来。如果你有的是电话网络，你在里面建立路径，那么拓扑细节就是一切。所以你必须详细了解拓扑，详细了解链路是如何分配的。而当你构建分组网络、应用 Paul 的思想时，拓扑根本不重要。再没有比它更无关紧要的了。拓扑只是分组穿过网络那一瞬间所看到的东西。

cues.en: Externally, you don't see anything but addresses. You want to name the destination note and nothing else. Since all the topological details were irrelevant in these packet networks, Vince says we can leverage that. If we have a common encapsulation format and a common address instruction, it only has to be common where two networks touch. So it's the time when borders start to matter. In telcos, there are no borders because there's only Ma Bell. There's only the telco.
cues.zh: 对外面来说，你看到的只有地址。你只想命名目标节点，别的什么都不用管。既然在这些分组网络里所有拓扑细节都无关紧要，Vince 说我们可以利用这一点。如果我们有共同的封装格式和共同的地址指令，那它只需要在两个网络相接的地方保持一致。所以，这时候边界开始变得重要了。在电信公司里没有边界，因为只有 Ma Bell。只有电信公司。

cues.en: But everybody can go and build their own networks, and we can transit them. We'll get the same transitivity that you get in a single network. So they wrote the specs for that in 74. And in 77, they demonstrated it by sending data from an SRI van over packet radio, over the ARPANET, over satellite, back through a
cues.zh: 但每个人都可以去建立自己的网络，而我们可以让它们互通。我们会得到和在单一网络中一样的传递性。所以他们在 74 年为此写了规范。到了 77 年，他们演示了这一点：从一辆 SRI 货车发送数据，经由分组无线电、ARPANET、卫星，再通过一个

cues.en: A whole bunch of gunk. But they were basically sending bits across the world and back again over a bunch of different networks using this concatenated networks idea. But VIN could never sell the Catanet name. It just had too many letters in it. The military likes three-letter acronyms, so it became TCPIP. And it won. It worked nicely.
cues.zh: 一大堆乱七八糟的东西。但他们基本上就是利用这种“拼接网络”的想法，让比特跨越世界，经过一堆不同网络再传回来。但 VIN 始终卖不出 Catanet 这个名字。它字母太多了。军方喜欢三字母缩写，所以就变成了 TCPIP。而且它赢了。它运作得很好。

cues.en: If you're doing this style of packet network, you nail all of the phone system problems. Now because on a packet by packet basis, you can choose alternate paths on failure rather than the system getting less reliable exponentially as it scales up. It gets more reliable exponentially as it scales up. Because as you make it bigger, there are more different ways to correct for a failure. So you flip the combinatorics around. You never set up anything. You just launch a packet.
cues.zh: 如果你采用这种分组网络，就能解决电话系统的所有问题。因为现在可以逐包处理，出故障时能选择备用路径，而不是系统规模扩大时可靠性指数级下降。规模越大，它反而越可靠。因为网络越大，纠正故障的不同方法就越多。于是组合关系就反过来了。你从不做任何建立，直接发一个包。

cues.en: If the network can't deliver it, it throws away. OK, I don't care. I'll launch another one. Because you're not doing any setup, you're completely bandwidth agnostic, because there's no setup to amortize. So you just end your packet. You don't have to make this strict hierarchical routing system that the telcos had to make. Whereas high bandwidth at the top, calls could take a maximum of five hops, which means three hops from the leaf to the center of the network, maximum that you would ever take.
cues.zh: 如果网络送不到，就把它丢掉。没关系，我不在乎，再发一个。因为你根本没做建立，所以完全不用关心带宽，因为没有建立开销需要分摊。所以你发完这个包就结束。你不必做电信公司那种严格的分层路由系统。那种系统是顶层高带宽，通话最多经过五跳，也就是从叶子节点到网络中心最多三跳，这就是你能走的最大跳数。

cues.en: They did that for stability and engineering concerns because it was the only network that they could control. And the core issue there is scheduling problems. All scheduling problems are NP-hard. And like the rest of us, they couldn't solve an NP problem. If you restrict it to a subdomain, particular subdomain being hierarchical allocation in a hierarchical bandwidth tree, you can solve the problem. Because you can aggregate things as you go up a tree and make sure you've got enough bandwidth for it.
cues.zh: 他们这么做是出于稳定性和工程上的考虑，因为那是他们唯一能控制的网络。核心问题是调度。所有调度问题都是 NP-hard 的。和我们其他人一样，他们也解不了 NP 问题。如果把它限制到某个子域——具体说，是在分层带宽树里做分层分配——那就能解决。因为沿树往上走时你可以做聚合，并确保带宽足够。

cues.en: IP network, arbitrary mesh. We don't need a hierarchy. We're not scheduling anything. You launch your packets. If the planet's aligned, it'll go through. It almost always goes through. And if it doesn't, then the end knows we'll fix it up. And we got one freebie. So those were the three known problems in the telco system that Baron was able to convince the glitter at ARPA. It was really important to make this.
cues.zh: IP 网络，任意网状。我们不需要层级，也不做调度。你把数据包发出去。如果一切刚好对齐，它就能过去；几乎总能过去。如果没过去，端节点知道，我们会把它修好。我们还白赚了一个。所以这些就是电信系统里的三个已知问题，Baron 说服了 ARPA 的那些精英。把它做出来真的非常重要。

cues.en: reliable, scalable system for military purposes. One thing they found when they deployed it was it got this adaptive routing that if there's a failure, you route around it. But that works from day one. From the time you plug something in, it's now a new element of the system. It can be used by the system and it can use it. So an IP network hooks itself up. A phone network does not hook itself up.
cues.zh: 一个用于军事目的的可靠、可扩展系统。他们部署时发现的一点是，它具备这种自适应路由：一旦出现故障，就能绕开故障。但这从第一天起就能生效。从你把某个东西插进去那一刻起，它就成为了系统的新元素。系统可以使用它，它也可以使用系统。所以 IP 网络能自己接通组网，电话网络不能自己接通组网。

cues.en: Phone networks are all about armies of people spending their lives in manholes punching down copper wires onto 50 blocks. And you don't ever do that with a packet network, because the addresses are explicit in the data. They're not implicit in the particular pattern of wires that are on the switch matrix. So I don't know if your network is open, but if it was, I could plug my laptop into the ethernet. It would be able to route packets out.
cues.zh: 电话网络靠的是成群的工人一辈子待在检修井里，把铜线打线接到 50 个接线块上。而分组网络从来不用这么做，因为地址明确写在数据里，而不是隐含在交换矩阵上那些连线的具体模式中。所以我不知道你们的网络是否开放，但如果开放，我就能把笔记本插到以太网上，它就能把数据包路由出去。

cues.en: because it would be able to route back to it. And I never punched down anything on a block. I never had to tell the network about my connectivity. I just need an address. And that makes it really easy for anybody to deploy the network. This is horrible for a telco, because it's a democratization. It moves a lot of their value out into commodity marketplace. You can just buy these devices and need them, and you don't need big company technicians to hook them up.
cues.zh: 因为它能路由回自己。而且我从没在配线架上打过线。我从不需要把连通性告诉网络。我只需要一个地址。这让任何人都能非常容易地部署网络。这对电信运营商很糟糕，因为这是一种民主化。它把他们的很多价值转移到商品化市场里。你只要买这些设备、用起来就行，不需要大公司的技术员来接线。

cues.en: But it was great for getting ubiquitous communication infrastructure. So like I said, TCP IP1, it was a terrific way of doing data networking. It is still a terrific way of doing networking. It nailed its problem so well that it's framed our thinking, just like the phone company framed our thinking. We now think of data communication as being IP data communication. It works.
cues.zh: 但它非常适合建立无处不在的通信基础设施。所以就像我说的，TCP/IP 是一种极好的数据组网方式。它现在仍然是一种极好的组网方式。它把自己的问题解决得太好了，以至于塑造了我们的思维方式，就像电话公司塑造了我们的思维方式一样。我们现在把数据通信就看作 IP 数据通信。它确实有效。

cues.en: problems that we're seeing today, the fact that our seamless connectivity isn't really seamless connectivity, that we have firewalls and VPNs, ad hoc synchronization protocols. They're not the failure of TCP. They're a success disaster. It's created this ubiquitous communication environment. Anything can talk to anything pretty easily, can hook itself up dynamically, can unhook itself.
cues.zh: 我们今天看到的问题，我们所谓的无缝连接其实并不真正无缝，我们有防火墙、VPN 和临时同步协议。这些不是 TCP 的失败，而是成功带来的灾难。它创造了这种无处不在的通信环境。任何东西都能轻松互通，能动态接入，也能自行断开。

cues.en: The network, the infrastructure all fixes itself up. Things like the web were put on top of it, which moved all of the world's information into digital form and made it accessible. And so now we've got this wealth of information. We have the widest to access it. We've got machines to access it. That was not the world that TCPIP was connected in, or it was created in. When it was created, machines were
cues.zh: 网络和基础设施都会自行修复。像 Web 这样的东西被架在上面，把全世界的信息转成数字形式并变得可访问。所以现在我们有了海量信息，有了最广泛的访问方式，也有了机器来访问它。那不是 TCP/IP 连接时或诞生时的世界。它诞生时，机器还是

cues.en: These huge things that lived in glass walled machine rooms, they had 1,000 people would use the same machine. There was two machines at MIT, and there were two machines at Berkeley. And there's one machine at Arizona where I went to school. Those machines would get connected together with wires. There wasn't a lot of data that you were putting in on card decks, and you were getting it out on printouts.
cues.zh: 这些庞然大物住在玻璃墙机房里，会有 1000 人共用同一台机器。MIT 有两台机器，Berkeley 有两台。亚利桑那有一台，就是我去上学的地方。那些机器用线缆连在一起。你通过打孔卡输入的数据并不多，输出则靠打印件。

cues.en: You wanted to be able to remotely use resources, and you occasionally wanted to be able to pull a card deck that somebody had put on the disk from their machine to your machine. But you had not a lot of information, a lot of users per machine, not a lot of machines. And that was the model of connectivity as this networking was being rolled out. It's kind of a bad fit today, and these are what I think of the problem.
cues.zh: 你想能远程使用资源，偶尔还想把某人放在他们机器磁盘上的卡片组拉到你的机器上。但你没有多少信息，每台机器上有很多用户，机器却没多少。网络铺开时，这就是连接模型。今天有点不合用了，而这些就是我认为的问题所在。

cues.en: The thing that annoys me most is that connected is this completely binary attribute. The internet is a thing, one thing, and you're hooked to it or you're not. No middle ground. And if you're hooked to it, this wealth of information is available to you. And if you're not hooked to it, you're hosed. And so if my PDA or my phone or my laptop aren't hooked to it, then I'm hosed. And I figure out some protocol to synchronize myself or download my mail ahead of time.
cues.zh: 最让我恼火的是，“已连接”完全是个二元属性。互联网就是一个东西，你要么连着它，要么没连，没有中间地带。连上了，海量信息就任你用；没连上，你就完蛋了。所以只要我的 PDA、手机或笔记本没连上，我就没辙了。我得琢磨出某种协议来同步，或者提前下载邮件。

cues.en: Getting connected to this global internet, because it's a single huge planet wide artifact, it's a pretty heavy duty operation. The only way you can do it is by getting this IP address that's globally known. You can get local NAT addresses, and there's some box at your border that turns that into a globally known address. But at the bottom, the protocol somewhere want a globally known address. And that address has to be.
cues.zh: 接入这个全球互联网，因为它是一个单一的、覆盖整个星球的庞大系统，所以是相当重的操作。唯一的办法是拿到一个全球已知的 IP 地址。你可以用本地 NAT 地址，边界上有个设备会把它转换成全球已知地址。但归根结底，协议在某个地方还是需要一个全球已知地址。而且这个地址必须……

cues.en: relatively stable. It's not an address that you can use for a millisecond and throw away. The world has to know where you are, and you have to know where the world is, which means that it has to be a topologically stable address. You have to know what the connectivity is around you. And the time scales, as we've scaled the network up, are pretty gross. The addresses have to be stable on the minutes to hours time scale. Otherwise, data just loops and black holes.
cues.zh: 相对稳定。这不是那种用一毫秒就能扔掉的地址。世界必须知道你在哪儿，你也必须知道世界在哪儿，这意味着它必须是一个拓扑稳定的地址。你必须知道周围的连通性。而且随着我们把网络规模扩大，时间尺度相当夸张。地址必须在分钟到小时的时间尺度上保持稳定。否则，数据就会打转，直接掉进黑洞。

cues.en: So those two things result in these three, that connecting to the net's a real heavy weight operation. That means that you want to carefully control those connections. Because of the topological stability requirement, the net hate things that move. You want to put a net on a train, well, good luck. There's a whole bunch of ad hoc infrastructure to do that. Put a net in your car, well, if the cell towers cooperate, maybe you can do it. But you're covering over the movement at layer two.
cues.zh: 所以，这两件事导致这三个结果：接入网络是非常重量级的操作。这意味着你要小心控制这些连接。由于拓扑稳定性的要求，网络讨厌会移动的东西。你想把网络放到火车上，那就祝你好运。要做这件事，得靠一大堆临时搭建的基础设施。把网络放进你的车里，如果基站配合，也许能行。但你其实是在二层把移动性掩盖起来了。

cues.en: And the neatest technology we've got today is broadcast. We've got all of these radios that are hooking things together. And we really can't use the suckers from our networking stack, because the net hates things that broadcast. The protocols weren't designed for it. The protocols were designed for a conversation between two applications on two machines. The conversations are point to point conversation. So we take all this data that's being broadcast out on our radios.
cues.zh: 如今我们最妙的技术是广播。我们有一大堆无线电把东西连在一起。而我们在网络栈里真的用不了这些家伙，因为网络讨厌会广播的东西。协议不是为此设计的。协议是为两台机器上的两个应用之间的对话设计的。这些对话是点对点对话。所以我们得处理所有这些通过无线电广播出去的数据。

cues.en: 10,000 radios hear it, and 9,999 throw it away. And only one will look at the data, because it's got his address. Now, maybe something like, hey, there's an accident two miles down on 101, that all 10,000 of those radios really cared about. But they have to ask individually. We got, in packet design, the company Bob and I were at, we got a chance to look at the data on the routers downstream of
cues.zh: 1 万台无线电收到了它，其中 9,999 台直接丢掉。只有一台会去看这份数据，因为里面写着它的地址。比如来一条：“嘿，101 号公路前方两英里出事故了”——这才是那 1 万台无线电都真正关心的消息。但它们得各自去问。在 Bob 和我当时所在的 Packet Design 公司，我们有机会查看路由器上的数据，这些路由器位于

cues.en: NBC's servers for the Olympics. At one time, their main router got severely congested. That's when Bodhi hit the pole on the slalom. In that router, there were 6,000 copies of the same data. Everybody was pulling down the URL. Poor router can't do anything about it. You can't optimize it because it's dynamic content. It's all going out in separate conversations.
cues.zh: NBC 奥运会服务器下游。有一次，他们的主路由器严重拥塞。就在 Bodhi 在回转滑雪中撞到旗门杆那会儿。那台路由器里有 6,000 份相同数据的副本。所有人都在拉取同一个 URL。可怜的路由器对此无能为力。没法优化，因为这是动态内容。这些数据都通过一个个独立会话来发送。

cues.en: All the router knows is I've got 6,000 separate TCP conversations. It's the same data. If you could broadcast it, you could turn that, both the router and the downstream links from the server reduce their bandwidth by three orders of magnitude. But our protocol architecture doesn't support that. It works at the conversation level. So I said this.
cues.zh: 路由器只知道我有 6000 个独立的 TCP 会话。这些其实是同一份数据。如果能把这份数据广播出去，路由器以及服务器的下游链路，都能把带宽需求降低三个数量级。但我们的协议架构不支持这一点，它是在会话层面工作的。所以我说了下面这段话。

cues.en: The success of the protocols changed the world. And when you get a new world, the protocols may not fit the new situation. It doesn't mean they're wrong. It doesn't mean that you aim the entire US research community at, oh, let's do a replacement for TCPIP. It's not the solution that's broken. It's the problem that that solution addresses has changed. There's a new problem. The change is this. When the protocols were rolled out,
cues.zh: 这些协议的成功改变了世界。而当你面对一个新世界时，协议可能不再适合新情况。这不代表它们错了。也不代表要把全美研究界都引向“来替换 TCP/IP 吧”。出问题的不是解决方案，而是这个解决方案所针对的问题已经变了。出现了新问题。变化是这样的。当这些协议被推出时，

cues.en: They got rid of the telco path building model. But the thing that the telcos enabled was conversations. When Bell first wrote out the phone system, he didn't know what the hell people were going to use it for. He just wanted to get phones out there. But there were no phones. You didn't have conversations with people on the other side of the planet because there was no technology for it. So he wanted to put these phones out and figure out how people were going to use them and what evolved towards phone calls.
cues.zh: 它们摆脱了电信运营商的路径构建模型。但电信运营商真正促成的是通话。贝尔最初设计电话系统时，根本不知道人们会拿它来干什么。他只想把电话推广出去。但当时还没有电话。人们无法和地球另一端的人通话，因为还没有这项技术。所以他想先把这些电话铺开，看看人们会怎么用，以及后来怎样演变成了电话通话。

cues.en: So in the 60s, people looked at it and said, oh, what we want to do is a different way of doing calls. We want this side effect in the phone system to actually be the centerpiece of our system. So when you design the TCP IP protocols, you make conversations be the central architectural element, as opposed to the phone system where they're what happens by accident after you build a path. So that was great. It got us going.
cues.zh: 所以到了 60 年代，人们看着它说：哦，我们想做的是另一种打电话的方式。我们想让电话系统里的这个副作用，真正成为系统的核心。所以在设计 TCP/IP 协议时，你让对话成为核心架构元素，而不像电话系统那样，对话只是你建好通路后偶然发生的事。这很棒，让我们起步了。

cues.en: But that's not how we use the network today. People don't want to have conversations. What they want is their web page. Any of the measurements that I've seen recently saying that the high 90% level of traffic is people trying to get some name chunk of data. They hand in a URL and they want to get something back. That's not a conversation. It's not a conversational model.
cues.zh: 但今天我们用网络不是这样的。人们不想要对话，他们想要的是自己的网页。我最近看到的任何测量都表明，90% 以上的流量都是人们在试图获取某个具名的数据块。他们递上一个 URL，想拿回点东西。这不是对话，也不是对话模型。

cues.en: It's sort of the computer equivalent of, does anybody have the time? Does anybody know where we are? That kind of interaction is a dissemination. It's a point to multi-point or multi-point to multi-point. It's a very efficient information transfer. It's been used for much longer than conversations. Conversations are a special case where the multi-points collapse to one. So it's a pure superset of the conversational model, but it's a different model.
cues.zh: 这有点像计算机里的“有人知道现在几点吗？有人知道我们在哪吗？”这种交互就是传播。它是点对多点或多点对多点，是非常高效的信息传输。它被使用的时间比对话长得多。对话是多点坍缩成一点的特殊情况。所以它是对话模型的纯粹超集，但又是另一种模型。

cues.en: So when you're doing a dissemination, what you're interested in is the data, not who gives it to you. Now, you can do disseminations over a conversational network. That's what we're doing. That's what we've been doing for a decade. It doesn't work very well in at least three important directions. The one that's biting us most today is you can't make a viable security model out of that.
cues.zh: 所以做传播时，你关心的是数据，而不是谁把数据给你。现在，你可以在对话式网络上做传播。我们正在这么做，已经做了十年。它至少在三个重要方向上效果不佳。今天最让我们头疼的是，你没法基于它建立可行的安全模型。

cues.en: Because if your network works in terms of conversations, in terms of virtual bit pipes, what you can secure in the network is that bit pipe. So we know how to armor an SSL connection. And I can armor the SSL connection to my mail server. But it doesn't stop the spam. Oh, good. These bits came from my mail server. They're garbage, but they came from my mail server.
cues.zh: 因为如果你的网络是按会话、按虚拟比特管道来工作，那你在网络里能保护的就是这条比特管道。我们知道怎么给 SSL 连接加防护。我可以给连接到邮件服务器的 SSL 连接加防护，但这挡不住垃圾邮件。哦，太好了。这些比特来自我的邮件服务器。它们是垃圾，但它们确实来自我的邮件服务器。

cues.en: The network has no knowledge of the content of what it means. So it can't do a security model at the network level because it's blinded the data. Like that NBC server, you get a tremendously inefficient network because the network can't distinguish the same content bound for different destinations. And so it can internally arrange to optimize the delivery of that content.
cues.zh: 网络不知道内容的含义，所以它没法在网络层做安全模型，因为它看不到数据。就像那个 NBC 服务器，你会得到一个效率极低的网络，因为网络无法区分发往不同目的地的相同内容，也就无法在内部安排优化这些内容的投递。

cues.en: doing something multi-point delivery. It can't leverage things like broadcast. It can't split data inside the topology, do flooding-style protocols. Because it doesn't know about the data. It knows about the conversations, the TCP IP headers that wrap the data. And up at the user level, we've got all of these apps that are dealing in dissemination-style data that want to deal in URLs, mail messages.
cues.zh: 做多点投递。它无法利用广播之类的方式。它无法在拓扑内部拆分数据，也无法做泛洪式协议。因为它不了解数据。它了解的是会话，是包裹数据的 TCP/IP 头部。而在用户层，我们有所有这些处理传播式数据的应用，它们想处理 URL、邮件消息。

cues.en: sensor readings, individual voice packets. And our network model is, OK, to write this app, I have to figure out what server to open a TCP conversation to. And it has nothing whatsoever to do with the app. It has nothing whatsoever to do with the problem that you're trying to solve. And so both the app writers and the users have to do this horrible plumbing operation in their head and in the network. If you've ever set up a VPN to get
cues.zh: 传感器读数、单个语音包。而我们的网络模型是，好吧，要写这个应用，我得弄清楚该跟哪台服务器建立 TCP 会话。这跟应用毫无关系。这跟你试图解决的问题毫无关系。于是应用开发者和用户都不得不在脑子里、在网络里做这种糟糕的管道操作。如果你曾经设置过 VPN 来

cues.en: at the internal websites or get your email when you're off site. You're doing this nasty, ugly plumbing to solve a problem that the network should be able to solve for you. But it doesn't know your intent. And it can't phrase what you want in terms of conversations. So if we wanted to do a more dissemination-based networking, the idea is you change your point of view to focus on the data, not where the data lives because it doesn't have to live anywhere. Data's named.
cues.zh: 访问内部网站，或在离开办公场所时收取邮件。你是在做这种讨厌又丑陋的管道工作，去解决一个网络本应能替你解决的问题。但它不知道你的意图。它也无法用会话来表达你想要什么。所以，如果我们想做更偏向传播式的网络，思路就是改变视角，关注数据，而不是数据存放在哪里，因为它不必存放在任何地方。数据是有名字的。

cues.en: When you want some chunk of data, you present its name to the network. And it doesn't matter what kind of networking technology you've got. Use them all. Does anybody know where we are? Pass this data out to the network. Hope somebody can give you a reply. Anything that's got the data, view it as broadcasting your request. If something's got the data, it can give it to you. If it's some kind agent like
cues.zh: 当你想要某个数据块时，就把它的名字提交给网络。你用的是什么网络技术都无所谓。把它们全用上。有人知道我们在哪儿吗？把这份数据发到网络上。希望有人能回复你。你可以把这件事看作是在向任何拥有这份数据的东西广播你的请求。如果某个东西有这份数据，它就能把数据给你。如果它是某种代理，就像

cues.en: the equivalent of a router that kindly forwards your packets. Instead, it could go get the data for you and then give it to you. The big issue in this is it's totally bogus, but right now, today, we decide that data is authentic if it comes from the server that originated the data. So I'm going to believe my copy of the New York Times front page, if and only if I get it from the New York Times server.
cues.zh: 相当于一个好心帮你转发数据包的路由器。它也可以改为替你去取数据，然后把数据交给你。这里的大问题是，这完全不靠谱；但如今，我们认定数据可信，只要它来自最初产生该数据的服务器。所以，当且仅当我是从 New York Times 服务器拿到我这份 New York Times 头版副本时，我才会相信它。

cues.en: got hauled halfway across the planet. They went through a lot of routers. They could easily have been corrupted. They cache reconstituted. I could be getting Fox News, for all I know. But our only model is you've got to secure the pipes. I think I would know if it was Fox News. But if you're going to data dissemination, where you get it from doesn't matter. It can't matter. You've got to be able to trust the data based on the data.
cues.zh: 这些数据被一路传到了半个地球之外。它们经过了很多路由器，很容易被篡改。它们可能被重新组装、缓存被重建。说不定我收到的就是 Fox News。但我们唯一能依据的模式是：必须保证管道安全。要真是 Fox News，我想我会知道。但如果你要做数据分发，数据从哪来并不重要。这不能有影响。你必须能仅凭数据本身来信任数据。

cues.en: doing some crypto things to the data so that you've got some basis for trusting it. And that actually works in general. That works in the face of proxies, staging data, doing lots of things. If you get the data, you look at it and say, yep, that's good stuff. No, that's bogus. So at the architectural level, if you're doing dissemination, you've got to have a security model. You've got to be able to assign things and make some sense out of them. Let me see if I can make that more concrete.
cues.zh: 对数据做些密码学处理，这样你才有信任它的依据。这在一般情况下确实有效。面对代理、数据暂存以及很多其他情况，这都行得通。你拿到数据，看一眼说：对，这是好东西。不，这是假的。所以在架构层面，如果要做分发，就必须有安全模型。你必须能给东西赋予标识，并让它们说得通。让我看看能不能讲得更具体。

cues.en: So the model is I do a request for today's New York Times. And I usually don't know what today is. So I want to make this generic request, give me today's New York Times. And I'm just sending that off into the ether, hoping that something's going to come back. So if I get back a response, it wants to have the name I request it, because that's used to vector the data to me.
cues.zh: 模型是这样的：我要请求今天的《纽约时报》。我通常不知道今天几号，所以我想发一个通用请求：给我今天的《纽约时报》。我就把它发出去，扔进虚空，指望能返回点什么。如果收到响应，响应里要带上我请求时用的名字，因为系统靠它把数据路由给我。

cues.en: The data's moving via diffusion. There's a request that sort of sets up the channel, and then data flows down that channel. So something is remembering that my port, at least someone had asked for New York Times, asked by the generic name. The data's actually got a specific name. Today's New York Times has got the data on it, and it's a particular web page. It's the front page. It's the starting point for getting the rest of the data.
cues.zh: 数据通过扩散来传输。先有一个请求把通道建起来，然后数据沿着这个通道流动。所以有东西记着我的端口，至少记得有人用那个通用名称请求过《纽约时报》。数据本身有一个具体名称。今天的《纽约时报》上带着数据，它是一个特定网页。它是首页，是获取其余数据的起点。

cues.en: And then down here is just the text to the front page. And there are two things that I've got to secure when I'm getting this data back. One is the binding of my generic name, Today's New York Times, to the specific name of really this edition of New York Times, the August 30, 2006 edition.
cues.zh: 下面这里就是首页的文本。我取回这些数据时，必须确保两件事。一是把我的通用名称“今日《纽约时报》”绑定到这一版《纽约时报》的具体名称上，也就是2006年8月30日版。

cues.en: And so I need some sort of authentication check in probably the associated certs that ties together those two names. NewYorkTimes.com has signed the fact that 2006-0830 index.html is an instance of NewYorkTimes.com today.
cues.zh: 所以我需要在相关的证书里做某种认证检查，把这两个名称绑定在一起。NewYorkTimes.com 已经签名确认，2006-0830 index.html 是今天的 NewYorkTimes.com 的一个实例。

cues.en: contract with the New York Times, I got their search. So I can look at that signature and say, yep, this really is from New York Times. It's not from Rupert Murdoch. And the other is the binding of this specific name to the data. So even if those two names are bound together, and I can say, oh, this packet came from the New York Times, but I need to know that Rupert didn't rip off the content and replace it with his own.
cues.zh: 和《纽约时报》签了合同，我拿到了他们的搜索服务。这样我就能看那个签名说：没错，这确实来自《纽约时报》，不是来自 Rupert Murdoch。另一件事是把这个具体名称绑定到数据上。所以即使这两个名称已经绑定在一起，我能说“哦，这个数据包来自《纽约时报》”，但我还需要知道，Rupert 没有把内容偷走并换成他自己的。

cues.en: I need that name binding to the data. The data itself, its real name is probably like a SHA-1 checksum, some cryptographic string of bits that represent the data. So it self-authenticates or self-identifies. But I need to take that identity, that SHA-1 of the data, and put it together with this name and bind them together with a cert. So that's what I mean by authenticating the data.
cues.zh: 我需要把这个名称绑定到数据上。数据本身真正的名字，大概就像 SHA-1 校验和，是一串代表该数据的加密比特串。所以它能自我认证或自我标识。但我需要拿到那个身份，也就是数据的 SHA-1，把它和这个名称放在一起，用证书把两者绑定起来。这就是我说的认证数据。

cues.en: And both the bindings and the data itself, all we ever do to get data is ask Google and then click on links. So you're following this path through meta information in order to get to the real information. You've got to verify the path if you're going to have any trust in the information. But when you're doing that, you don't have to change very much. So this was the New York Times web page.
cues.zh: 不管是绑定还是数据本身，我们获取数据的方式无非是问 Google，然后点链接。所以你是在沿着一条穿过元信息的路径，最终拿到真正的信息。如果想信任这些信息，你就得验证这条路径。但做这件事时，你不需要改太多东西。所以这就是 New York Times 的网页。

cues.en: And this is some goop that I added on so that I could authenticate these bindings. But the page self-identifies. I can shawl one any web page. This stuff doesn't have to be packaged with it. I can stick this somewhere else and separately get the credentials and get the data. So I could make an appliance that I sit at the edge of the network that handled dissemination for me and would at least give me the benefits of broadcast and distribution over.
cues.zh: 这是一些我额外加上的东西，用来认证这些绑定。但页面会自我标识。我可以把它附加到任何网页上。这些内容不必和它打包在一起。我可以把它放在别处，单独获取凭证并取到数据。所以我可以做一个设备，放在网络边缘，替我处理分发，至少能让我获得广播和分发的优势，覆盖

cues.en: enterprise campus size things without changing any infrastructure. Basically, it's collecting data, collecting credentials where it can, pushing them together, and sending this out on the wire in response to requests. So it's a nice incremental deployment, a nice overlay way of laying out networks, because what we're doing today is dissemination. We just can't trust it. So top level design philosophy is
cues.zh: 企业级、园区级规模的东西，而无需改动任何基础设施。基本上，它是在收集数据，尽可能收集凭证，把它们整合起来，并在收到请求时通过网络发送出去。所以这是一种很好的增量部署，一种很好的网络叠加布局方式，因为我们今天做的就是分发。我们只是无法信任它。所以顶层设计哲学是

cues.en: Data's got a name, not a location. When I say this, it's really hard talk to give. When I've tried to give it before, the first thing I get asked is, but this is just caching. And it's not. The effect is very much the same, but your point of view is completely different. In caching, you say, oh, the data lives there, but I've got a copy of it here. And my model is the data doesn't live anywhere.
cues.zh: 数据有名字，没有位置。我这么说时，这其实很难讲清楚。以前我试着讲时，第一个被问到的是：但这不就是缓存吗。并不是。效果非常相似，但你的视角完全不同。在缓存里，你会说，哦，数据住在那里，但我这里有一份副本。而我的模型是，数据不住在任何地方。

cues.en: Wherever it is, it's great. Wherever I get it, I can authenticate it. I know whether or not I can trust it. I can ask the world, anybody got this data? And I don't care where it is. And that's not caching, because I'm not moving it from its one true location to some other location. It doesn't have one true location. You can only do that if you do the second. Integrity and trust are properties of the data, not of the way that you obtain it.
cues.zh: 不管它在哪儿，都行。无论我从哪儿拿到它，我都能验证它。我知道它是否可信。我可以问全世界：有人有这个数据吗？我不在乎它在哪儿。这不是缓存，因为我不是把它从唯一的真实位置搬到另一个位置。它没有唯一的真实位置。只有做到第二点，你才能这样。完整性和信任是数据本身的属性，而不是你获取它的方式。

cues.en: And you have to be able to develop integrity and trust from the data itself. So this is by contrast to, say, the Microsoft Authenticode model, where you download this update from Microsoft, and there's a little window that comes up and says, do you trust Microsoft? And the answer is no. I kept clicking no, and my machine never got updated. I don't.
cues.zh: 而且你必须能够从数据本身建立完整性和信任。所以，这跟比如 Microsoft Authenticode 模型相反：你从 Microsoft 下载更新，弹出一个窗口问：你信任 Microsoft 吗？答案是不信任。我一直点“不”，我的机器就再也没更新过。我不信任它。

cues.en: Their model is, do you trust their delivery mechanism? They're basically asserting, installing this update won't cause financial harm to Microsoft. Great. But that's not what I want. I want my machine to work. I want to know what you're going to do to my machine. I want to know something about the data and the operations you're going to take. But they can't tell me that. So I want properties of the data where I don't have to trust remote agents. That the data itself.
cues.zh: 他们的模型是：你信任他们的交付机制吗？他们本质上是在断言：安装这个更新不会给 Microsoft 带来财务损失。很好。但那不是我想要的。我想要我的机器能正常工作。我想知道你们会对我的机器做什么。我想知道你们要处理的数据和要执行的操作。但他们没法告诉我这些。所以我要数据本身具备一些属性，让我不必信任远程代理。也就是数据本身。

cues.en: Let's me figure out what it means and who sends it, how it's connected to the world. And there's always been this tension in the CS community between different ways of moving bits. So the telco people move bits over these hardwired connections. They don't need any buffers because they have a master clock in Kansas that schedules everything on their network. So things never interfere. They all have their little dedicated time slots and they move around.
cues.zh: 让我弄清楚它是什么意思、是谁发送的、它如何与世界相连。计算机科学界在“如何移动比特”的不同方式之间，一直存在这种张力。电信公司的人通过硬连线连接来传输比特。他们不需要任何缓冲区，因为他们在堪萨斯有一个主时钟，调度其网络上的所有事情。所以事情永远不会互相干扰。它们都有自己专属的小时隙，并在其中移动。

cues.en: Their religion was the only true bits are bits in a wire. And when these data networking people came along and they put in buffers because they didn't want to schedule, so data may land at the same place in the same time, and that's great. You turn some of those bits in a wire to bits in a memory, put the others on the wire, and then you take the ones out of the memory, and the phone people look and go, buffers, that's not networking. Networking is cut through. Networking is moving the bits to the wire.
cues.zh: 他们的信条是：唯一真实的比特，就是线路上的比特。后来这些做数据网络的人出现了，他们加了缓冲区，因为不想做调度，这样数据就能在同一时间落到同一个地方，这很棒。你把线路上的一些比特变成内存里的比特，把其余的留在线上，然后再把内存里的取出来；电话行业的人一看就说：缓冲区？那不算网络。网络是直通。网络就是把比特送到线路上。

cues.en: Those bits that sit in a memory, those aren't real bits. And then the networking people would say, oh, those people do databases. They've got data on disk. We do networking. We do distributed computation. So there's way too much religious fundamentalism already in this country. There is no one job. Bits are bits. They're all good.
cues.zh: 那些待在内存里的比特，不是真正的比特。然后做网络的人会说，哦，那些人搞数据库，数据放在磁盘上；我们做网络，我们做分布式计算。所以这个国家已经有太多宗教原教旨主义了。没有唯一的工作。比特就是比特。它们都很好。

cues.en: Moves, bits, I don't care if it's a disk, a wire, memory, USB stick, running around on your bicycle. Great. If you move bits, time or space, you're part of a network. You're doing a good thing. So you get some wins if you do things this way. One is the communication win. And you can do way more inside the network on behalf of users. Because you're communicating to the network what you want.
cues.zh: 移动比特，我不管它是磁盘、网线、内存、U 盘，还是你骑着自行车到处跑。很好。只要你移动的是比特、时间或空间，你就是网络的一部分。你是在做一件好事。这样做能带来一些收益。其中之一是通信上的收益。你能在网络内部替用户做更多事。因为你在告诉网络你想要什么。

cues.en: rather than some meaningless abstraction. I say, I want this data. And it can be something in the name that tells you even more about the data. I want the contents of my mailbox in a way that's secure, implicit in the fact it's the contents of my mailbox. If I'm not on our fired wall network, make a VPN to get it for me. If I can say the intent at the top level, I can do things lower down to concept the right semantics.
cues.zh: 而不是某种无意义的抽象。我会说：我想要这份数据。名字里还可以包含一些信息，告诉你更多关于这份数据的事。我想要我邮箱里的内容，而且方式要安全；这其实已隐含在“它是我邮箱内容”这一点里。如果我不在我们的防火墙网络上，就给我建个 VPN 去取。如果能在顶层表达意图，我就能在底层做事情，来落实正确的语义。

cues.en: Most of the problems that we have in congestion today, we've got this high bandwidth core because a fiber holds terabits, much more data than we have available to send. We've got these skinny tails that connect us out to us. And all the congestion that you tend to see when you're networking is congestion from the core to you along this tail. But the end of that tail where the data lives is in your service provider's world.
cues.zh: 如今我们遇到的大多数拥塞问题，都来自高带宽的核心——因为一根光纤能承载数太比特，远远超过我们要发送的数据量。我们有这些细尾巴，把网络接到我们这里。而上网时你看到的拥塞，基本都是沿着这条尾巴、从核心到你这里的拥塞。但这条尾巴的末端、也就是数据所在的地方，是在你的服务提供商那边。

cues.en: And you're sitting in your home PC world. And you can exactly control the data you send to him, so you never have a congestion issue. You can always send what's most important first. But you have no way to say what he should send to you. And because of that, I wait for hours while my son's gaming traffic is piled up on the network headed down our link. And my email is way more important than his gaming traffic, at least to me.
cues.zh: 而你坐在家里的 PC 世界里。你可以完全控制自己发给他的数据，所以从来不会遇到拥塞问题。你总能把最重要的内容先发出去。但你没办法决定他该发什么给你。正因如此，我儿子游戏流量堆积在网络上、沿着我们的链路下行时，我得等上好几个小时。而我的邮件可比他的游戏流量重要多了，至少对我来说是这样。

cues.en: I would like to be able to, and I pay the service provider, so I would like to be able to say to the service provider, send my stuff first. But there's no protocol for that. And the people that want to do QoS are the service providers. They want to make it end to end, because they can extort more money out of Google if they say, oh, no. Pay us for end to end quality of service. Otherwise, I deep-six all your bits, or half of them at least.
cues.zh: 我希望能这样，而且我是向服务提供商付费的，所以我想能对服务提供商说：先发我的数据。但没有这样的协议。而想做 QoS 的是服务提供商。他们想把它做成端到端的，因为只要他们说“哦不，给我们付端到端服务质量的钱”，就能从 Google 那里榨出更多钱。否则，我就把你所有比特都丢掉，至少丢掉一半。

cues.en: And they're not interested in making the tails any better, because that's just really small. I don't have much money. Google's got way more. So go after the big target. So you get an architectural focus and sort of the wrong kind of QoS, things that will make things better. If you're doing dissemination, you get data in response to a question you ask. So it's really request response. That doesn't mean stop and wait. You can ask a lot of questions in parallel. But the order of your questions is
cues.zh: 他们也没兴趣改善尾部，因为那实在太小了。我没多少钱，Google 的钱多得多。所以要盯就盯大目标。于是你得到的是架构层面的关注，以及某种错误类型的 QoS，而不是真正能改善情况的东西。如果你做的是信息分发，你提出问题后会得到数据作为响应。所以它其实是请求-响应。这不意味着停等。你可以并行提出很多问题。但你提问的顺序就是

cues.en: the order of importance. So if I can arrange on my local network that I always ask for my email before my son's gaming traffic and I run the gateway, then I will get good service from the email. And it's entirely in my control, because I can control the requests. What happens when you do dissemination, because there's this symmetry. It's not a pipe from the.
cues.zh: 重要性的顺序。所以如果我在本地网络上能安排成：总是先请求我的邮件，再请求我儿子的游戏流量，而且网关由我控制，那我就能让邮件获得好服务。而这完全在我掌控之中，因为我能控制请求。当你做信息分发时会发生什么，因为存在这种对称性。它不是一根从……来的管道。

cues.en: service provider to you down which bits are blasted and you have absolutely no control over it. Instead, you get a fine-grained control at the data item level, because you're asking for things individually. And we don't have the Olympic server problem. The network is dealing entirely in content. It's not having 6,000 separate conversations about Bodhi's pole incident. That's just one main piece of content. So you can distribute it as efficiently as you need to.
cues.zh: 服务提供商会决定哪些比特被推给你，而你完全无法控制。相反，你在数据项级别获得细粒度控制，因为你是逐个请求内容的。而且我们没有“奥运服务器问题”。网络完全以内容为处理对象。它不会围绕 Bodhi 的 pole 事件进行 6000 个独立会话。那只是一个主要内容项。所以你可以按需高效地分发它。

cues.en: no matter how dynamic it is. So this already said, you get rid of a lot of religion. Bits are bits. The bits in a wire, and the bits in a memory, and the bits in a disk. As long as you can name them uniformly, you access them uniformly. And so you don't have to do the moral equivalent of GNOME VFS, where you put in this huge application layer to try and accomplish the same thing. You put it in at the network architecture layer.
cues.zh: 不管它有多动态。所以前面已经说过，你能摆脱很多教条。比特就是比特。线路里的比特、内存里的比特、磁盘里的比特。只要你能统一命名它们，就能统一访问它们。这样你就不必做 GNOME VFS 的精神等价物——塞入一个巨大的应用层来试图完成同样的事。你把它放到网络架构层。

cues.en: Since you're not talking to nodes anymore, the reason that you're there is not so you can have an intimate one-on-one with google.com. Instead, you're just presenting this URL and saying, help, somebody find it. There's much less need for global topologies, global naming, particularly
cues.zh: 既然你不再是在跟节点对话，你在那里并不是为了和 google.com 单独一对一交流。相反，你只是把这个 URL 摆出来，说：帮帮忙，谁把它找出来。对全局拓扑、全局命名的需求就小得多，尤其是

cues.en: When you're doing something that's really local, like a sensor network, if I wanted to know what the temperature in this room was, or if I wanted to know directions to the nearest espresso machine, the room could be broadcasting it to me. And it wouldn't need to IP wrap it. It could just be information that was wrapped in MAC layer encapsulations. And I can use proximity and diffusion and very simple local protocols in order to move that information around. Because you don't care about the topology. You just care about the data.
cues.zh: 当你做的是真正本地的事情，比如传感器网络，如果我想知道这个房间的温度，或者想知道去最近的咖啡机怎么走，房间可以直接广播给我。而且它不需要用 IP 封装。它可以只是封装在 MAC 层里的信息。我可以用邻近性、扩散和非常简单的本地协议来把这条信息传开。因为你不关心拓扑。你只关心数据。

cues.en: And similarly, since we don't care about data of living for a time in buffers or on disk, we can still access it by name. We don't have a conversation where there's always a real-time aspect. The fact that you've got intermittent connections doesn't matter. You can still get all the data. If anybody remembers it, they can give it to you. So security terms, since you're making
cues.zh: 同样，既然我们不在乎数据在缓冲区或磁盘上停留一段时间，我们仍然可以按名称访问它。我们不需要始终带有实时性的会话。你只有间歇性连接也没关系。你仍然可以拿到所有数据。只要有人记得它，就能把它给你。所以从安全角度说，既然你在构建

cues.en: Trust, be architectural. It's really easy at the network level to make farming and fishing and spam and all of these imposter attacks or unintended sender attacks. They're just impossible. Because you can tell from the data that you've got who sent it, what it is. You can never do that in a connection network. By its design.
cues.zh: 信任，应当架构化。在网络层面，让域欺骗、网络钓鱼、垃圾邮件以及所有这些冒充攻击或非预期发送者攻击变得不可能，其实很容易。它们根本不可能发生。因为从你拿到的数据中，你能看出是谁发送的、它是什么。在连接型网络中，你永远做不到这一点。这是由其设计决定的。

cues.en: A conversational network wants to be completely agnostic to its data. It wants to be transparent. It's built that way from the ground up. You want to be able to ship anything over a TCP connection. When the protocol was designed, it was important to make it completely agnostic. But if it's completely agnostic, then you can't do a trust model. Anything can be in that pipe, and you don't control the other end. You're putting the trust in.
cues.zh: 对话式网络希望对自己的数据完全无感知。它希望保持透明。它从底层就是这样构建的。你希望能通过 TCP 连接发送任何东西。设计协议时，让它完全无感知很重要。但如果完全无感知，就没法做信任模型。管道里可以是任何东西，而你不控制另一端。信任得由你自己放进去。

cues.en: the data and user level objects and the stuff that you ask for. So you don't care whether you got it over SSL. That's not going to help. And this is purely hypothetical, but if some big, greedy phone company wanted to extort money from you, they have a lot of trouble doing that if you can communicate over anything that moves, literally anything that moves. You say, hey, you're not going to move our bits. No problem. There's a plane flying overhead. It's got a disk in it.
cues.zh: 数据、用户级对象，以及你请求的那些东西。所以你不在乎是不是通过 SSL 拿到的。那也帮不上忙。纯属假设，如果某个贪婪的大型电话公司想勒索你，只要你能通过任何会动的东西通信——字面意义上任何会动的东西——他们就很难得逞。你说，嘿，你们别想搬走我们的比特。没问题。天上正飞着一架飞机，里面装着磁盘。

cues.en: My bits go up, they go to the other side, they come down. I don't care. Anything that moves bits, I'm flooding the data. So if they don't get there on your wires, they'll get there on somebody else's wires. It's like the original IP network where you could bomb the hell out of it and it kept working. On this network, you can QS the hell out of the center and it keeps working. Because the network doesn't matter much anymore. The way that you're moving bits around is this global diffusion process.
cues.zh: 我的比特往上走，到了另一端，再下来。我不管这些。只要能搬比特，我就把数据灌进去。所以就算你的线路不通，它也会走别人的线路。就像早期的 IP 网络，你怎么炸它都还能继续跑。在这个网络里，你可以往中心拼命灌 QoS，它照样能跑。因为网络本身已经不太重要了。你搬运比特的方式，就是这样一个全局扩散过程。

cues.en: So there's a little bit of stuff to figure out in order to do this. There's some stuff that's probably pretty easy because it's all been done. One is being able to check the integrity of data just based on the data. Well, that's something that we had to figure out for privacy-enhanced mail. There's already a worked example, probably not the greatest example. It's a much more limited context. But at least a problem of this nature has been solved in a fairly convincing way.
cues.zh: 要做到这一点，还有些东西得想清楚。有些可能挺简单，因为都已经做过了。其中之一是仅凭数据本身就能校验数据的完整性。这个我们当年做保密增强邮件时就得解决。已经有现成的范例，可能不是最好的范例，适用范围也窄得多。但至少这类问题已经以一种相当有说服力的方式解决过了。

cues.en: And the trust structure that you need to embed it in, that's also been worked out. So there was this complete disaster foisted on us called certificate hierarchies that have never worked. And they have no trust at all associated with them. Two years ago, VeriSign sold a root certificate to Microsoft to some unknown party still floating around. You basically can't trust.
cues.zh: 而要嵌入它所需的信任结构，也已经设计出来了。可偏偏有人硬塞给我们一个彻头彻尾的灾难，叫证书层级结构，从来就没管用过。而且它们身上根本没有半点信任可言。两年前，VeriSign 把一张根证书卖给了 Microsoft，又转手到某个不知名的机构，至今还流落在外。你基本上没法信任。

cues.en: The people in which you impose, in a certificate hierarchy, the root, you've got to have ultimate trust. But these are people that make their money selling stuff. They have a lot of minimum age workers. It's really hard to put ultimate trust in that economic structure. You can get, via things like Subram's Web of Trust, get much more distributed community action.
cues.zh: 在证书层级结构里，你指定为根的那些人，你必须给予终极信任。可这些人靠卖东西赚钱，还雇着一大批拿最低工资的工人。真的很难把终极信任寄托在这样一种经济结构上。而通过 Subram 的 Web of Trust 这类机制，你能得到分布程度高得多的社区协作。

cues.en: And so if you use PGP models, you can get some pretty good trust in things. You don't want the web to be any harder than it is today. So we've got a model for creating content that is you stick data in a directory somewhere, and now you've created content. Keep it that model. But I want to be able to trust that data. I want to get some of these signatures. But that's OK. Make the repository do it.
cues.zh: 所以，如果用 PGP 模型，你就能对内容建立相当不错的信任。你不希望 Web 比现在更难用。我们已经有了一种创建内容的方式：把数据放进某个目录，内容就算创建好了。保持这种方式。但我希望能信任这些数据。我想拿到这些签名。不过没关系，让仓库来做这件事。

cues.en: If you've got the permissions to shove the data in the repository, that should be enough permissions to attach a search to the data that says, OK, I will attest to the fact that this is the data that was put into this repository at this time. I'm not going to tell you that it's good data, but I tell you that, yes, this is the legitimate copy that was first created under this URL. So there are models for how to do that.
cues.zh: 如果你有权限把数据塞进仓库，那也就应该有足够权限给数据附加一条声明：好，我证实这些数据是在这个时间被放进这个仓库的。我不会说它是好数据，但我会告诉你，是的，这是最初在这个 URL 下创建的合法副本。所以，这件事是有模式可循的。

cues.en: Park's working on a system that they call Usable Security, kind of an umbrella project. They've got a model for how to do repositories in that automatic way that they call Instant PKI. And UT Austin has been doing some wonderful things in distributed networking, peer-to-peer networks, very distributed services. They have an instant BitTorrent model that they call SnakeBite. It's actually being funded under Google Summer of Code.
cues.zh: Park 正在做一个他们称为 Usable Security 的系统，算是一个总括性项目。他们有一个以自动化方式做仓库的模型，称为 Instant PKI。UT Austin 在分布式网络、点对点网络和高度分布式服务方面做了一些很棒的工作。他们有一个即时 BitTorrent 模型，叫 SnakeBite。它实际上是由 Google Summer of Code 资助的。

cues.en: that has a similar sort of repository, but also registry models that are in it. So I think you could sort of do a high speed collision between these two and get secure, absolutely painless entry. And then lastly, you've got to be able to find stuff. Well, Google's nailed this problem. Nobody remembers URLs. Nobody keeps bookmarks anymore. What you do is remember some search terms, and you type them into Google, and then you search the page to find out what you want.
cues.zh: 它也有类似的仓库，但里面还有注册表模型。所以我觉得，可以把这两者来个高速碰撞，得到安全、完全无痛的入口。最后，你还得能找到东西。这个 Google 已经搞定了。没人记得 URL 了。也没人再保存书签了。你要做的是记住一些搜索词，把它们输入 Google，然后搜索页面，找出你想要的内容。

cues.en: So start with that model. Maybe you've got a URL. Maybe you search. If you've got some information that you want to spread around or some queries you want to spread around, we've got a lot of ways of doing that in this kind of model. Epidemic algorithms, which we've used for years on directories. Directed diffusions, where you set up channels to constrain the amount of data that leaks outside the path where it's wanted.
cues.zh: 所以，从那个模型开始。也许你有一个 URL，也许你会搜索。如果你有想传播的信息，或者想扩散的查询，在这种模型里我们有很多办法。流行病算法，我们在目录上已经用了很多年。定向扩散，你设置通道来约束泄漏到目标路径之外的数据量。

cues.en: You can use small world graphs so that you can do very efficient data location for subsets of data, anything where you can define a center. So there's a lot of themes that some smart people might be able to figure out, not me. Since you're getting everything by names, you want to spend a lot of time on exactly what is a name and how you want to do naming. Biggest thing is you want all your content to be immutable once it's created. It goes out in the world and you've lost control over it.
cues.zh: 你可以使用小世界图，从而对数据子集做非常高效的数据定位，只要能定义中心就行。所以这里有很多主题，聪明人也许能想明白，我不行。既然你通过名字获取一切，就要花很多时间想清楚：名字到底是什么，以及你想怎么做命名。最重要的是，你希望所有内容一旦创建就不可变。它一旦发布到世界上，你就失去了对它的控制。

cues.en: It's now out in the world. That means that if you want to update something, what you do is supersede it with a newer version. And that newer version should reference back to the old version and say, hi, I'm a newer version of the New York Times, when you've got is probably obsolete. That means that wherever the data is, you can use it. You may have to do some work to find out that you've got the most recent copy or the most recent copy that's accessible to you. But you can use all the copies that are out there.
cues.zh: 它现在已经散布到外部世界了。这意味着，如果你想更新某个东西，你要做的是用更新的版本取代它。而那个更新的版本应回指旧版本，并说：嗨，我是《纽约时报》的更新版本，你手上的那份很可能已经过时了。这意味着，无论数据在哪里，你都可以使用它。你可能要费点功夫，才能确认自己拿到的是最新副本，或是你能访问到的最新副本。但你可以使用外面存在的所有副本。

cues.en: So to do that, you want to be able to put sequence and time information, version number information into names. That's easy, but something that you need to do and tie into the verification authentication machinery. You don't ever want to send huge things across the network. You want to take huge things and split them up into small pieces. It's good for the
cues.zh: 所以要做到这一点，你需要能把顺序和时间信息、版本号信息放进名称里。这很容易，但这是你需要做、并接入验证和认证机制的事情。你永远不想通过网络发送庞大的东西。你要把庞大的东西拆成小块。这有利于

cues.en: network for the users of the network because if you've got a lot of small pieces and you've got a lot of paths, you can send the different pieces over different paths and get much higher effective bandwidth, potentially much higher reliability. It's good for the user because the user gets way more control. Because you're asking for things a piece at a time, you don't have to wait for the entire download of this week's GCC to come down before you can get the next packet in your VoIP call. Everything's little pieces.
cues.zh: 网络和网络用户，因为如果你有很多小块，又有很多路径，就可以把不同小块走不同路径发送，从而获得高得多的有效带宽，也可能有高得多的可靠性。这对用户也有好处，因为用户能获得多得多的控制权。由于你是一次请求一小块，所以不必等本周的 GCC 整个下载完，才能收到 VoIP 通话里的下一个数据包。一切都是小块。

cues.en: that are handled more or less independently. And then we've got lots of memory everywhere, so we put the pieces back together and do a big thing at the end. And as long as you can do the segmentation and we dealt with it in the naming, then the real-time media, I was co-author on the RTP, on the VoIP protocol, that was designed as a dissemination protocol because we were worried about going through voice gateways, about recording conferences on disks, and replaying them.
cues.zh: 这些处理起来多少是相互独立的。然后我们到处都有大量内存，所以最后把各个部分重新拼起来，做一件大事。只要你能做分段，并且我们在命名中处理了它，那么实时媒体——我是 RTP、VoIP 协议的合著者，它被设计成一种分发协议，因为我们担心要经过语音网关、把会议录制到磁盘上并重放。

cues.en: Every little voice packet, every little video packet's got a time stamp and a sequence number on it so that anybody can reconstruct the entire conversation. And it doesn't matter where you get it from. And it doesn't matter what the temporal characteristics of the medium are, because the time information's all explicit in the data. And I'm sure I've got a slide that says that over again. That's kind of a general statement. If you look at the big advance that packet switching made over
cues.zh: 每个语音小包、每个视频小包都带有时间戳和序列号，这样任何人都能重建整个对话。你从哪里拿到它都无所谓。媒介的时间特性是什么也无所谓，因为时间信息全都明确写在数据里。我确信我还有一页幻灯片又讲了一遍这个。这算是个概括性的说法。如果你看看分组交换取得的巨大进步，相较于

cues.en: circuit switching, there's a lot of information that's completely implicit in a circuit system. The time slots that each piece of data goes through, they're never known by the data. The destination of the data is never known by the data. All that you send across the wires is the actual data itself, but no addressing, no meta information. If you're doing that, then you can't possibly
cues.zh: 在电路交换中，电路系统里有很多信息是完全隐含的。每份数据经过哪些时隙，数据本身永远不知道。数据的目的地是什么，数据也永远不知道。你在线路上发送的只是实际数据本身，没有寻址，也没有元信息。如果这样做，那你根本不可能

cues.en: repair from failures because the data isn't idempotent. It doesn't tell you anything about itself. It doesn't tell you where it's going. It doesn't tell you what path it's going to follow. So you can't fix the path for it because you don't know the path for it. The big advance in packet switching, one of Paul's first insights was put addresses on the packets. Yeah, you use a few bits, but you get this massive increase in reliability because now every packet tells you where it's going and where it came from.
cues.zh: 因为数据不是幂等的，所以没法从故障中恢复。它不告诉你任何关于自身的信息。它不告诉你它要去哪里。它不告诉你它会走哪条路径。所以你没法定它的路径，因为你不知道它的路径。分组交换的巨大进步，Paul 最早的洞见之一，就是把地址放到数据包上。是的，你用几个比特，但可靠性大幅提升，因为现在每个包都告诉你它要去哪里、从哪里来。

cues.en: And so now, wherever you are in the network, you know what to do with the sucker. You know if it's for you or if it's not for you. You know where it's going so you can figure out a way to get it there. So making implicit information explicit suddenly enables a whole bunch of new functions, new use cases. It's easy to screw this up. So when ATM, the telcos networking, they put identifiers in their little 54-byte cells, but they used
